outline: Respiratory failure/respiratory arrest and pulmonary vascular disorders
Metabolic, regulatory, and structural disorders — disorders of gas exchange
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (pulmonary arteriovenous fistula) producing an anatomic intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt
mechanism: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation directly connects a branch of the pulmonary arterial circulation with the pulmonary venous circulation, allowing a fraction of deoxygenated venous blood to bypass ventilated alveoli and the pulmonary capillary gas-exchange interface. This anatomic right-to-left shunt raises the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient and produces hypoxemia that improves poorly even when inspired oxygen concentration is markedly increased because the shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas.
vignette: A 29-year-old woman with recurrent spontaneous epistaxis and small telangiectasias on the lips and fingertips is evaluated for exertional dyspnea and cyanosis. Contrast-enhanced chest imaging shows a direct vascular communication between a branch of the pulmonary artery and a pulmonary vein. Arterial blood gas analysis shows hypoxemia with an increased alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient. Her arterial oxygen tension rises only modestly while she breathes 100% oxygen.
lead: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's persistent hypoxemia despite the marked increase in inspired oxygen concentration?
correct: A portion of venous blood bypasses ventilated alveoli through a direct pulmonary artery-to-vein connection and then mixes with oxygenated pulmonary venous blood
distractors: Blood traverses alveoli with reduced ventilation relative to perfusion, producing a low ventilation-perfusion ratio
Oxygen equilibration is slowed by increased thickness of the alveolar-capillary diffusion barrier
Global alveolar ventilation is reduced, lowering alveolar oxygen tension without increasing the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient
Ventilated alveoli receive little or no perfusion, increasing physiologic dead space
distractor_notes: Low V/Q regions can cause hypoxemia and an increased A-a gradient, but increasing inspired oxygen generally improves oxygenation because blood still passes capillaries adjacent to ventilated alveoli. In an anatomic right-to-left shunt, some blood never contacts alveolar gas, making the hypoxemia substantially less responsive to oxygen.

Diffusion limitation can increase the A-a gradient when oxygen transfer across an abnormal alveolar-capillary membrane is impaired, but the presented structural lesion is a direct artery-to-vein channel that bypasses the membrane entirely. Supplemental oxygen can increase the diffusion driving pressure in diffusion-limited disease.

Pure alveolar hypoventilation lowers alveolar and arterial oxygen tension together and characteristically has a normal A-a gradient. This patient has an increased A-a gradient and an anatomic vessel that bypasses alveolar gas exchange.

High V/Q or dead-space physiology occurs when ventilation is present but perfusion is deficient. A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation does the opposite with respect to oxygenation: blood is perfused through a vascular shortcut that bypasses ventilated alveoli and the capillary gas-exchange surface.
key_expl: The vascular connection is a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (pulmonary arteriovenous fistula). It creates an anatomic intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt: deoxygenated pulmonary arterial blood reaches the pulmonary venous circulation without traversing alveolar capillaries. Raising inspired oxygen markedly increases alveolar oxygen tension in ventilated units, but it cannot oxygenate the fraction of blood that bypasses those units. The resulting admixture therefore produces an increased A-a gradient with hypoxemia that is notably resistant to correction with supplemental oxygen.
objective: Explain why a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation causes oxygen-resistant hypoxemia: deoxygenated blood bypasses ventilated alveoli through an anatomic right-to-left intrapulmonary shunt and mixes with oxygenated blood.
clues: recurrent spontaneous epistaxis and mucocutaneous telangiectasias
direct pulmonary artery-to-pulmonary vein vascular communication
only modest improvement while breathing 100% oxygen
